k6 is an open-source load testing tool
that allows you to create a bunch of
virtual users that will continuously
make a series of HTTP requests and
gather statistics about how long it
takes for those requests to resolve
there's a paid cloud-based version that
can help manage test runs and provide
some nice visualizations but the
open-source version can be run locally
for free and that is what I'll be using
here in order to design a test that is
representative of actual traffic to your
website k6 allows you to convert an HTTP
archive or har file into a testing
configuration to record a har file you
can open up chrome and go into the
developer tool section under the network
tab you then load a page or series of
pages and save the file by
right-clicking and selecting save all as
har with content now that we have the
har file we can use the k6 convert
command to turn this into a testing
configuration file that will be the
input to k6 when we run it if we look at
this test file we see that all of the
network requests made by chrome were put
into this array which would be loaded as
a batch HTTP request by each virtual
user by default the test configuration
will have a single virtual user and load
the test page just one time we can
modify the configuration to match the
desired load profile by editing the
relevant sections for example we could
set up the test to have an on-ramp
period of 30 seconds where we transition
from 0 to 50 virtual users followed by a
minute of constant load at 50 virtual
users and finally an off ramp period
back down to zero load when designing
the test it is useful to think about how
long a normal user would wait between
page loads and adjust how long the
virtual user will wait accordingly if
your goal is to test that initial
onslaught of users from a large traffic
spike you probably want to make this
delay quite small but if you want to
simulate a sustained load you can set
this delay to something longer or even
add some randomness to it to account for
the fact that all users won't behave
identically
now that we have the configuration ready
we just need to execute the k6 run
command and pass it the javascript test
configuration file k6 will run for the
specified amount of time and then output
some statistics about key metrics as you
can see the output contains many
different metrics but i think the most
important one here is the HTTP request
total duration which includes the time
spent sending the request waiting on a
response and then receiving the data
within that response we also may want to
consider not just the average times
reported but also the upper percentile
time such as the 90th percentile or 95th
percentile to get a sense of how the
full set of users may be impacted by
load so that represents a basic website
load test using k6 and can be adapted to
test a variety of different scenarios
one common use case for something like
this would be to integrate a load test
into a continuous integration pipeline
to measure how new features are
impacting performance before merging
them into the master branch and
releasing them to the public
